title: Tasting at the Master level
lead: The same deductive grid as Advanced, held to a higher bar: six wines in 25 minutes with vintages, how to calibrate with a tasting group, reading age and producers, and what the Court means by a classic wine.

intro.title: SIX WINES, ONE SYSTEM
intro.text: The grid doesn't change at Master level. The wines get harder and the calls get finer.

lines.label: The format
lines.text: Six wines in 25 minutes, spoken to a panel. Name the grape, country, district and appellation, and vintage where it applies.

lines.label: The grid
lines.text: Advanced and Master share one format: Sight, Nose, Palate Structure, Palate, then Initial and Final Conclusions.

know: The Court's About page says the flight is three whites and three reds.
The final conclusion takes one vintage, plus an official quality level and style category where they apply.
Tasting feedback is split into Sight, Nose and Palate, Structure and Conclusions, and counts grapes named correctly by color.
Master-level flights can include unpublished classics, newly established wines, aged whites and reds, sweet wines and subtler classics.
The Court's feedback: taste the wine in the glass, not your idea of it, and work the method before trusting recognition.

lines.label: Practice
lines.text: The Court's feedback asks for the full grid on every wine, even one you recognize, and a reason behind every call.

lines.label: Groups
lines.text: Group mentoring is encouraged. Timing each other and pointing out missed boxes is fine; staging a copy of the exam is not.

know: For every box, ask what could have caused it, and what the wine could be given everything said so far.
Taste wines that share an aroma compound side by side, such as peppery rotundone in Syrah, Grenache and Grüner Veltliner.
Taste less obvious wines, blind and sighted, and drink across the range of any grape that trips you up.
Keep tasting aged, sweet and sparkling wines, beer, spirits and sake with the method, not only six-in-25 drills.
Court mentors may time you and note missed areas, but may not share point weights or a list of possible wines.

lines.label: Age in the glass
lines.text: Color, fruit condition, fruit against savory notes, and sediment point to an age range. Élevage, wine law and vintage knowledge narrow it to one year.

lines.label: Producers
lines.text: A classic region has many iconic producers that share core traits. Taste across producers, not just one.

know: The Court's conclusions guide judges the age range from fruit condition, color, fruit versus savory notes, and sediment.
For the vintage, it applies typical élevage, wine law and regional vintage knowledge.
Wine Folly: red pigment fades from deep ruby and violet toward paler red and orange, and eventually brown.
With age, fruit turns from fresh to dried or stewed, and acidity and tannin fade (Wine Folly).
The Court's classic session: a warm vintage can give red Burgundy riper fruit, more alcohol and more forward oak.

sections.name: What classic means
sections.source: Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas: What Makes a Wine Classic (mentoring session slides); Advanced Sommelier Level Wines

lines.label: The idea
lines.text: A classic shows a distinct, repeatable set of traits from a renowned place: the benchmark other wines of that grape are judged against.

lines.label: Your list
lines.text: The Court publishes a core wine list for Advanced. At Master level you build your own list of classics beyond it.

know: Three tests: a unique, distinctive flavor profile; an established quality level; a global market presence.
The checklist asks whether the region shows its traits in all but the most unusual vintages.
It asks for a quorum of iconic producers whose wines share traits despite their house styles.
A wine must also fit the deductive exam fairly and consistently; one 'no' and it doesn't qualify for the exam.
Some regions keep an original style and add an equally valid modern one; others become classic within a few decades.

facts.fact: The tasting is scored on clearly and accurately describing six different wines within twenty-five minutes, identifying where appropriate grape varieties, country of origin, district and appellation of origin, and vintages.
The About page describes the tasting as six wines tasted blind in 25 minutes, three red and three white, done verbally before a panel of Master Sommeliers.

The 2024 Advanced and Master Sommelier Deductive Tasting Format is one grid for both levels: Sight (clarity, color intensity, primary and secondary color, rim variation, staining, tearing, gas), Nose (faults, intensity, age assessment youthful/developing/vinous, fruit, fruit condition, non-fruit, earth, mineral, oak), Palate Structure (sweetness, acidity, alcohol, body, phenolic bitterness for whites, tannin for reds, texture), Palate (confirm from the nose; balance, length, complexity).

Initial Conclusion: possible grape varieties; climate cool, moderate or warm; possible countries; age range 1–3, 3–5, 5–10, 10+ years. Final Conclusion: grape or blend, country, region and appellation, official quality level (e.g. Village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru, Reserva, Riserva, Kabinett, Spätlese) and official style category (e.g. Trocken, Sec, Moelleux, SGN) where appropriate, and one vintage.
MS Tasting feedback reports Sight, Nose & Palate, Structure and Conclusions, and grapes correctly identified (white and red).

MS Tasting feedback comments: use a consistent ordered method; rely on the full Deductive Tasting Method, not recognition; reserve instincts for wines you have trouble with; taste the wine, not your idea of wine; change a wine only with a clear reason.

MS Tasting preparation suggestions: break down the grid box by box; if you recognize a grape, fill out the entire grid every time with full descriptors; drink a wide spectrum of troublesome varieties; give possible reasons for each sensory evaluation and confirm on reveal; taste wines with shared impact compounds (Syrah, Grenache and Grüner Veltliner share pepper from rotundone); for every box give the descriptor and ask what could have caused it and what the wine could be; keep tasting aged, dessert and sparkling wines, beer, spirits and sake; don't get mired in '6 in 25'.
MS Theory feedback tasting suggestions: taste less obvious wines, blind and knowing what they are; for any wine, list 5 other classic or established producers.
Master-level flight considerations: published and unpublished classics, newly established, aged wines (white and red), sweet wines (table and fortified), subtler versions of long-established wines.
Because the CMS does not re-certify, the deductive tasting demands that candidates make their own list of classic wines beyond what the Court has published.

Classic criteria: a unique and distinctive flavor profile (grape, specific to one region, sole combination of characteristics); an established quality level (within grape, category, gastronomy world); global market presence (consumers and professionals, history and lore, iconic producers).

Deductive tasting qualifications include: unique combination of visual, olfactory and structural traits; among the most renowned expressions; unique growing circumstances and established winemaking apparent in flavors; unique and similar traits in all but the most idiosyncratic vintages; history and connection to place; a quorum of iconic producers with similar traits regardless of style; established global presence; the wine can be shown fairly and consistently in the exam. A wine that doesn't check yes on all boxes doesn't qualify for the deductive exam, though it may have merit for service, theory or business.

The session quotes a definition of a classic wine as one with time-honored, exemplary traits (colors, aromas, flavors, textures) that set the standard against which other wines of the same variety are judged; and advises tasting a range of producers in every region, not just one.

Categories in the session: Established; Original vs Modern (e.g. original Napa Cabernet: pyrazines, moderate plus alcohol and astringent tannins, fruit just ripe, oak less forward; modern: subtler pyrazines, high alcohol and rounder tannins, overripe or liqueur-like fruit, oak more forward); Stuck in the Middle (e.g. a pumped-up red Burgundy from a warm vintage: riper fruit, medium plus alcohol, more oak, too youthful for earth); Newly Established (Etna Rosso DOC); On the Radar (Rueda Verdejo DO). Wines can become classic in a few decades.
The Advanced Sommelier Level Wines list is the Court's published list of core grapes for the Advanced tasting.

Conclusions guide: age range from fruit condition, color or lack of it, focus on fruit or savory elements, and any sediment; vintage from typical élevage, wine law knowledge and regional vintage knowledge; climate from fruit condition and structure such as acidity and alcohol.
Theory answer guidelines: vintage ratings by media may be asked on a specified scale (usually 1 poor to 5 excellent).
The MS resource guide lists vintage references (e.g. Oz Clarke's Vintage, Broadbent's Vintages) and top wine lists as resources supporting tableside theory.

Wine Folly: red color changes from deeper ruby and violet to paler red and orange, eventually a dull translucent brown; fruit moves from fresh and tart to dried or stewed; acidity and tannin fade; heightened acidity and tannin act as a runway for aging.

Mentoring guidelines: group mentoring is encouraged; mock examinations simulating CMS-A exams are prohibited; tasting sessions should not mirror exam situations exactly; timing candidates, sharing methodologies and noting missed grid areas are encouraged; sharing point weighting or a specific list of possible wines is prohibited; fees for exam mentoring outside Court courses are prohibited; training wines and questions are tools, not an indication of exam content.

unverified: The three whites and three reds split is stated on the Court's About page, not on the exam page; it is given with that attribution.

The classic-wine material comes from a Court mentoring-session slide deck (file dated 11-2022, session dated December 2024), not from an exam standard. Named producers and the speakers quoted in it are left out.
Wine Folly's notes on how color, fruit and structure change with age come from one article's tastings and are a general guide, not a rule for every wine.
The Court gives no fixed list of Master-level tasting wines; none is implied here.

read.bigIdea: Same grid as Advanced. Harder wines, finer calls.
read.where: The Master tasting is **six wines in 25 minutes**, described aloud. The grid is the one you used at Advanced. What changes is the flight: aged, sweet, subtle and newer **classics**, and a **vintage** for each.

stops.name: Description
stops.text: **Sight**, **Nose**, **Palate Structure** and **Palate**, in order. The score rests on describing each wine **clearly and accurately**.

stops.name: Initial conclusion
stops.text: Possible grapes, **climate** (cool, moderate or warm), possible countries and an **age range**: 1–3, 3–5, 5–10 or 10+ years.

stops.name: Final conclusion
stops.text: One grape or blend, the country, **region and appellation**, the official **quality level** and **style category** where they apply, and **one vintage**.

stops.name: Feedback
stops.text: Results split into Sight, Nose and Palate, Structure and Conclusions, with grapes named correctly by color. The Court's advice: rely on the **method**, not recognition, and change a call only with a clear reason.

read.mixup: The **initial conclusion** gives possibilities: grapes, countries, an age range. The **final conclusion** commits: one grape, one place, **one vintage**.

read.bigIdea: Calibrate the method, not your memory.
read.where: At Master level a tasting group keeps everyone honest. The Court's feedback examples and its **mentoring guidelines** show what good practice looks like, and where it stops.

stops.name: Full grid, every time
stops.text: If you know the grape, fill out the **whole grid** anyway, with descriptors and where they come from. It ties what you taste to **theory**.

stops.name: Two questions per box
stops.text: For each box: what could have caused this, and what could the wine be, given everything said so far? Then check your reasons at the reveal.

stops.name: Taste across boundaries
stops.text: Line up wines that share a compound, like peppery **rotundone** in Syrah, Grenache and Grüner Veltliner. Drink the full range of any grape that trips you up, and keep tasting aged, sweet and sparkling wines, beer, spirits and sake.

stops.name: Keep it fair
stops.text: **Group mentoring** is encouraged, and so are timing and noting missed boxes. Court mentors may not share **point weights** or a list of possible wines, or run **mock exams** that copy the real one.

read.mixup: A **study group** times you and calls out missed boxes. A **mock exam** that copies the Court's setup is off-limits for Court mentors.

read.bigIdea: Age is a range first, then one year.
read.where: The Master tasting names **vintages**, so age has to be read, then pinned down. The Court's conclusions guide sets the order: describe, reason to an **age range**, then commit to **one vintage**.

stops.name: Read the age
stops.text: Use **fruit condition**, color, fruit against **savory** notes, and **sediment**. Wine Folly notes that red color fades toward orange and brown, fruit turns dried or stewed, and acid and tannin soften.

stops.name: Pin the vintage
stops.text: Apply typical **élevage**, the region's **wine law** and **regional vintage knowledge**. Pick the year that fits everything you described.

stops.name: Know the weather
stops.text: A warm year can push a classic off type. The Court's example is a red Burgundy with riper fruit, more alcohol and more oak, too young to show earth.

stops.name: Know the producers
stops.text: A classic region has a quorum of **iconic producers** sharing core traits despite house styles. Taste many of them, or you learn one producer instead of the region. For every wine, name five classic producers.

read.mixup: **Age assessment** on the nose is youthful, developing or vinous. **Age range** in the initial conclusion is in years: 1–3, 3–5, 5–10 or 10+.

keyPoints.line: A classic has a flavor profile no other place repeats.
It holds an established level in its grape and category.
It has market presence, history and iconic producers.
Master candidates build classics past the published list.

read.bigIdea: A classic is a benchmark you can taste blind.
read.where: The Court doesn't hand Master candidates a list. Its **classic** checklist gives you the questions instead, so you can judge any wine, now and as classics change.

stops.name: Distinctive
stops.text: Is the **flavor profile unique**? Look at the grape, the one region and the combination of traits.

stops.name: Established quality
stops.text: Does it hold an **established quality level** within its grape, its category and the world of food and wine?

stops.name: Global presence
stops.text: Do guests and professionals know it? Is there **history**, and a quorum of **iconic producers**?

stops.name: Fit for the exam
stops.text: It must show its traits in all but odd **vintages** and fit the deductive format fairly. One 'no' and it isn't an exam classic, though it may still matter for service and the list.
